I think my personal story might help explain a little.

Here's why I got started: when I was young, I used to dress up like Bible book characters for the kids at my church. When kids would sit around and listen to the story of some anthropomorphized character, or a Bible story containing an animal (like the beaten donkey), I would barge in the door right as the story ended and the kids would scream joyously and flock to me. I adored being in costume.

Fast forward to me at 14. I'm sitting in a hospital, something's horribly wrong. I've attempted suicide from the pain many a times, and the doctor comes in with a lot of news. None of it good. One of those tidbits is that I will never be able to have my own children. It's just not feasible. My dreams of growing up, getting married, and having kids like all my mothers before me are gone.

Now, fast-forward again. I'm 17. I'm debating between a full-ride art college and going into engineering. We know what my parents want, and I can't blame them. Me and my artsy friends from my newfound full-ride art school are talking (Regent University--Christian college in VA Beach) and one of them mentions how her favorite projects are fursuits. "What?" I had never heard this term before. She quickly reels a little, noting that she does it "for the kids". I pry a little, and soon I'm hearing stories of how her mascoting around and making all these children smile. It's exactly what I used to do back in my church, but she made her costume and made the character. I get a little bit of flashbacks to how much I miss working with children.

Fast forward to a mere few years ago, I'm in college for Engineering. The glorious mascot is a wolf, and our team is terrible. But the number of families at our games is astounding, and everyone is friendly as can be. I draw anthropomorphic creatures in my spare time through engineering school to keep my art talent alive, and I meet a group of "wolf mascots" who make their own suits and go entertain the children in the family section while the game waits to begin. You'd better believe I get in on that. I walk around in a suit, and children are so happy to see me. I take the "head" off to chat with their parents--sometimes the dad's are "you're dad should be so proud his daughter is an engineer" and others are flabbergasted at my progress in such a cutthroat school. But they all know who I am, and are fine with me playing a few rounds of cornhole with their kids and get pictures with the not-mascot before giving some other kids some attention.

As for the other members, really the most notable with me is my friend who specializes in working with special needs children. She regularly uses animals for therapy, and using a mascot suit has a similar effect. Mute children suddenly have so much to say, shy children run up and grab hold of the fake tail, and kids who have trouble focusing suddenly are wholly attentive on this giant wolfy-thing. She's able to get these kids to come out of their shells and experience the moment, which in her line of work every moment like that means progress.

I'm since graduated, but I personally see my "suited" self as a way to entertain both myself and my peers. Sometimes, I can sit around a group of artists and talk about the construction of these crazy suits. Other times, I'm in it entertaining children and talking to parents (so they don't feel like there's some creepy stranger walking around) and I always respect their boundaries. It brings me back to days before my life had a bit of a crash, perse, and lets me enjoy the company of children again without having that haunting feeling of how I'll never have my own. I spend time speaking to my friend about the merits and demerits of the approach for autistic children and how best to respond to various "stimming" in order to help them when I encounter them (in or out of character). Other times, I talk about the long arduous process of creating a character to my furry peers, and ask them about how they "got here". Lastly, I use my characters to hone my skills in acting, storytelling, and character-building which I will need for my personal end-goal, which is to be a game designer.

Is that enough to make the whole community seem like a potential gain? Probably not, but I meet more people like--who do it with no morally questionable intentions--than I do the "yiffers". As much as it seem the entire furry community is full of sexual degenerates and messy personalities, many of us really are quite "normal" with unusual circumstances that brought us to love the community or find value in it.

However, as hinted at above, the sentiment is what's important: in this age of twisting morals and "anything goes" degeneracy, we need to raise alarm at these sorts of things. If that is the language that gets people's attention, then so be it. More importantly, though, it's about trying to convince people to keep away from the ideals in the first place since they do no good for Catholoc ideals.
